Japan has successfully conducted its first-ever live launch of a U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missile from the JS Chokai, an Aegis-equipped destroyer fitted with Mk 41 vertical launch systems. The exact Tomahawk variant used was not disclosed.
With this launch, Japan became the third country, after Australia and the Netherlands, to fire a Tomahawk missile from a surface warship outside the U.S. Navy.
Japan plans to acquire up to 400 Tomahawk missiles, 200 Block IV and 200 Block V variants, for an estimated $1.03 billion.
By the end of the current program, five of Japan's eight Aegis destroyers are expected to be capable of launching Tomahawk missiles: JS Chokai, JS Kirishima, JS Haguro, JS Myoko, and JS Atago.

According to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat, Russia has resumed using North Korean Hwasongpho-11Ga (Hwasong-11A) tactical ballistic missiles, better known as the KN-23, against Ukraine.
Early battlefield wreckage analyses and tracking data from 2024 showed that the missile performed poorly. Early production batches suffered from guidance and manufacturing flaws, resulting in a reported circular error probable (CEP) of around 800–1,000 meters, and in some cases even missing targets by several kilometers. By comparison, Russia's Iskander-M has a CEP of about 5–10 meters.
Following its poor performance, North Korea reportedly introduced a series of upgrades to the Hwasongpho-11Ga. These improvements are believed to have reduced the missile's CEP to around 100–200 meters, with later versions reportedly achieving a CEP of as little as 1–5 meters.
